subject: arabic
license: Our own (written for Waymark). Examples are deck ids only; the deck stays private (ADR 0011).

data.title: No word for “is”
points: In the present, Arabic has no word for am, is or are. You put the two parts side by side: “I ready” is “I’m ready”.
A question is the same words, with your voice rising at the end.

data.title: My, your, his: endings
points: My, your and his are endings on the word: ism (name) → ismi, my name.
A word ending in -a shows a t before the ending: gahwa (coffee) → gahwitak, your coffee.
The same endings go on other words too: wēn (where) → wēnik, where are you (to a woman)?

data.title: Counting things
points: Two of something is one word with -ēn on the end: dagīga (a minute) → dagigtēn, two minutes.
From 3 to 10, a short form of the number comes before the plural: talāta (three) → talat layāli, three nights.
A plural that starts with a vowel takes a t after the number: ayyām (days) → xamas tiyyām, five days.
From 11 up, the word stays singular.

data.title: il-, “the”, and the sun letters
points: “The” is il- in front of the word: xēr (good) → ilxēr.
Before the sun letters, the l becomes the next sound, said twice: il + šams → iššams, the sun. You still write the lām; a shadda marks the doubled letter.
In Palestinian, j often counts as a sun letter too: ijjaww, the weather.
data.letters: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن

data.title: fī, “there is”
points: There is and there are are one word, fī, in front of the thing: fī ɧáda 3a -lbāb, someone is at the door.
Asking is the same words with a rising voice: fī wāyirlis hān? Is there wifi here?
There isn’t is fiš (or mā fī): fiš ɧadd, no one.

data.title: bidd-, “want”
points: Want is bidd- with the endings from chapter 2: bíddi, I want; bíddak, you want. It also means need.
Then the thing you want: bíddak kōla? Would you like some cola?
Or what you want to do, in the verb’s plain form: bíddi ʔarūɧ, I want to go.

data.title: The present: b-
points: A verb in the present starts with b-, and a sound after it says who: baɧíbb, I like; biɧíbb, he likes.
The same form says what you do in general and what you’re doing now: baštíɣil dawām kāmil, I work full-time.
A second verb drops the b-: baɧíbb asāfir, I like to travel. After bidd- too: bíddi ʔarūɧ.
table: you like (to a man); she likes

data.title: dān, ríjil: feminine with no -a
points: Most feminine words end in -a, but a few don’t. Many are parts of the body that come in pairs: dān, ear; ríjil, leg or foot; īd, hand; 3ēn, eye. šámis, the sun, is one too.
A describing word after them takes -a anyway: dān maxzūga, a pierced ear.
Hebrew does the same with יד and רגל.

data.title: 3ind-, “have”
points: There’s no verb for have. You say “at me”: 3índ- with the endings: 3índi, I have; 3índak, you have.
Asking is the same with a rising voice: 3índak wlād? Do you have any children?
I don’t have: mā 3índi.

data.title: mā…š and miš, “not”
points: A verb is made negative with -š on the end, and often mā in front: baɧíbb → baɧíbbiš, I don’t like.
Anything that isn’t a verb takes miš in front: miš mnīɧ, not good; ána miš mihtámm, I’m not interested.
You’ve met two already: fī → fiš, there isn’t; 3índi → mā 3índi, I don’t have.

data.title: The past
points: The past has endings instead of b-. Its plain form is “he did”: kátab, he wrote. That’s the first form the word path gives you for a verb (kátab, yíktib: he wrote, he writes).
The other people are endings on it. The -t of I and you is often said -it: dafá3it, I paid.
Two kinds of verb bend a little. A doubled verb takes -ēt: ɧaʈʈ (he put) → ɧaʈʈēt, I put. A verb with a long ā shortens it: nām (he slept) → nimt, I slept.
table: I wrote; you wrote (to a man)

data.title: She, and the -a ending
points: Most words for a woman, or a thing that counts as feminine, end in -a: ustāz → ustāza, a teacher (a woman).
A describing word takes -a after a feminine word: kbīr → kbīra, big; ɧábba kbīra, a big pimple. Things in the plural take it too: maɧallāt ɧílwa, nice shops.
Colors have their own feminine: áɧmar → ɧámra, red; áxɖar → xáɖra, green; ábyaɖ → bēɖa, white; áswad → sōda, black.

data.title: The future: ɧa-
points: For what’s going to happen, put ɧa- in front of the verb, in place of the b-: ɧanām, I’m going to sleep.
It works for everyone: ɧatílbis, you’re going to wear; ɧatūlad, she’s due (going to give birth).
Many speakers say raɧ instead, as a word of its own: raɧ anām. The two mean the same.

data.title: múmkin and lāzim: “can” and “must”
points: Can I…? Could you…? is múmkin before a verb in its plain form: múmkin āxud kubbāyit máyya? Can I have a glass of water?
Must, need to is lāzim, the same way: lāzim aštíɣil, I need to work.
Neither word changes: the verb after it shows who. Add law samáɧit, please, to be polite.

data.title: Me, you, him: endings on verbs
points: The endings from chapter 2 also go on verbs, for who it’s done to: baɧíbb → baɧíbbak, I love you.
Me is -ni on a verb (not -i): būsni, kiss me; bitɧúkkni, it itches (me).
It and them take -u, -ha and -hum, like his, her and their: bitɧíbbha, you like it (a feminine thing).

data.title: kān: “was” and “used to”
points: Was is kān, with the past endings: kunt, I was; kānat, she was.
There was is kān fī: kān fī bárig, there was lightning.
kān before a present verb says what someone was doing, or used to do: kunt tʂáyyiɧ? Were you crying?
table: I was; you were (to a man)

data.title: ílli: “who”, “which”, “that”
points: One word joins a description to a thing or a person: ílli. ilwálad ílli bi-nnúʂʂ, the child who’s in the middle.
On its own it means the one who, or what: min ílli gúltu, of what you said.
When the thing is what the verb is done to, the verb takes an ending for it: ilʔaflām ílli bitɧíbbha, the movies you like (them).

data.title: ákbar: “bigger”, “more”
points: Comparing words have one shape: kbīr → ákbar, bigger; ʂɣīr → áʂɣar, smaller; ktīr → áktar, more.
Than is min: ákbar mínni, older than me. The word doesn’t change for a woman or for several.
Before a noun it means the most: áʂɣar wāɧad, the youngest one; áktar barnāmij, the favorite program.

data.title: Commands
points: A command to a man is the verb with no b- and no sound for who: íʈla3 fōg! Come upstairs! xūd šmāl! Turn left!
To a woman add -i, to several add -u: íʈla3i, íʈla3u.
Don’t is mā with the you form of the present, or -š on it: mā tínsa! Don’t forget! tiɧkīš! Don’t talk!

data.title: gā3id: “right now”
points: To say something is going on right now, put gā3id before the present verb: gā3id bágra, I’m (busy) studying.
It changes like a describing word: gā3id for a man, gā3da for a woman or a feminine thing, gā3dīn for several.
On its own it means sitting, or off work: ána gā3id, I’m off work.

data.title: Verb shapes: your binyanim
points: Like Hebrew, Arabic builds verbs from a root in a few set shapes. If you know the binyanim, you already know how these work.
A doubled middle letter makes a verb do more, or make someone do it, like piʿel: dáras, he studied → dárras, he taught. Hebrew does the same with למד and לימד.
t- in front of that shape is done to or for yourself, like hitpaʿel: it3állam, he learned; atdárrab, I practice.
in- in front is something that happens to you, like nifʿal: inwálad, he was born (נולד); inkásar, it broke (נשבר).
table: a-: like hifʿil (less common in speech)

data.title: Plurals inside the word
points: Hebrew adds -im or -ot. Arabic often changes the vowels inside the word instead: bēt → byūt, houses; kalb → klāb, dogs.
These are learned with the word: that’s why a word’s card shows its plural in brackets.
Some words do take an ending: -īn for groups of people (m3allim → m3allimīn, teachers), -āt for many others (sayyāra → sayyārāt, cars).
Plural things count as feminine (chapter 11): maɧallāt ɧílwa, nice shops.

data.title: law: “if”
points: If is law: law má3i maʂāri, if I have money.
law samáɧit, “if you allow”, is please.
yā rēt law… is I wish: yā rēt law 3índi sayyāra, I wish I had a car.

data.title: lámma and 3ašān: “when” and “because”
points: When is lámma: lámma ʔajū3, when I get hungry.
Because, and so that, is 3ašān: 3ašān tit3állam 3árabi, so that you learn Arabic. With an ending: 3ašānni, because I.
la-ʔínn- also means because: la-ʔínni batmárran, because I exercise.

data.title: kull: “every”, “all”
points: kull before a word with no il- is every: kull yōm, every day.
Before a plural with il- it’s all: kull liɣrāɖ, all the things.
kull 3ām w ínta b-xēr, “every year and you’re well”, is said for birthdays and holidays.

data.title: ɧāl-: “yourself”; bá3ɖ: “each other”
points: Myself, yourself is ɧāl- with the endings: ɧāli, ɧālak. intíbih 3a ɧālak! Take care (of yourself)!
kēf ɧālak? “How is yourself?” is How are you? ɧāsis ɧāli… “I feel myself…” is I feel…
Each other is bá3ɖ: btígrabu la-bá3ɖ? Are you related (to each other)?

data.title: Question words
points: A question word usually comes first, and the rest stays in the same order as the answer: šū ísmak? What’s your name?
kam takes a singular word: kam wálad? How many children? gaddēš asks how much: gaddēš 3umrak? How old are you (how much is your age)?

data.title: xúbiz, xúbza: -a for one
points: Some foods and plants are named as a whole, with no -a: xúbiz, bread; bēɖ, eggs; šájar, trees.
Add -a for one of them: xúbza, a slice or a loaf; bēɖa, an egg; šájara, a tree.
The one with -a is feminine (chapter 11): bāɖat bēɖa, she laid an egg.

data.title: Telling the time
points: What time is it? is gaddēš issā3a? The answer is issā3a and the hour: issā3a talāta, it’s three.
Past the hour is w, “and”: talāta w rúbi3, a quarter past three. To the hour is ílla, “but”: árba3a ílla rúbi3, a quarter to four.
The twenty minutes is a third, tilt: talāta w tilt, twenty past three.

data.title: w, bass, wálla, ínnu: the joining words
points: And is w, said with the next word: ána w ínta, me and you.
bass is but, and also just: baɧíbb áɧɖar riyāɖa bass mā bál3abha, I like watching sports but I don’t play; bass ɧúʈʈu dagigtēn, just put it in for two minutes.
Or is aw; in a question it’s wálla: jāhiz wálla líssa? Ready, or not yet?
That, after think or say, is ínnu: aʐúnn ínnu…, I think that…

data.title: líssa and min gábil: “still”, “yet”, “already”
points: líssa before a word is still: ána líssa ja3ān, I’m still hungry.
Before a negative verb it’s not yet: líssa mā wíʂliš, he isn’t here yet. A question can end … wálla líssa? … or not yet?
Already is min gábil after the verb: (i)tɣaddēt min gábil, I’ve already eaten lunch.

data.title: gábil and bá3id: “before” and “after”
points: Before is gábil, after is bá3id, in front of a word: bá3id la3b ilkōra, after playing soccer.
In front of a whole sentence they take ma: gábil ma tdūb, before it melts; bá3id ma xállaʂ, after he finished.
gábil hēk is before (now): 3úmrak sāfarit gábil hēk? Have you ever traveled before?

data.title: maslūg, maftūɧ: the done-to shape
points: Many describing words say something was done to the thing, with ma- in front and a long ū: maslūg, boiled, from sálag, to boil; maftūɧ, open, from fátaɧ, to open; maksūr, broken, from kásar.
Verbs that end in a vowel give ma…i: mágli, fried; mášwi, grilled.
It comes after the thing: bēɖ maslūg, a boiled egg; bēɖ mágli, a fried egg.
Hebrew’s paʿul shape does the same. Hebrew פתוח is maftūɧ.

data.title: fōg, taɧt, jamb: where things are
points: Words for where go before the thing: fōg ilkánaba, over the sofa; jamb ilmamárr, next to the aisle.
On their own they’re places: íʈla3 fōg! Come upstairs!
They take the endings too: jambi, next to me; guddāmak, in front of you.

data.title: ilbēt ilkbīr: il- on both
points: A describing word comes after the thing: bēt kbīr, a big house.
When the thing has il-, so does the describing word: ilbēt ilkbīr, the big house; ilʔákil ilɧarrāg, the spicy food.
Without the second il-, it’s a sentence: ilbēt kbīr, the house is big (chapter 1: no word for is).

data.title: kubbāyit máyya: “of” by putting words together
points: A glass of water is two words side by side: kubbāyit máyya. Hebrew does the same: כוס מים.
A first word ending in -a shows its t: kubbāya, a glass, becomes kubbāyit; dáraja becomes dárajit (dárajit ilɧarāra, the temperature).
The first word never takes il-; for “the”, il- goes on the last word: kílmit issírr, the password.

data.title: min and la-ɧádd: “since” and “until”
points: min is since: ána 3āyiš fi ɣázza min ilʔalfēn w 3ášara, I’ve been living in Gaza since 2010.
The verb stays in the present, where English says I’ve been living. Hebrew does the same.
la-ɧádd is until, before a thing: la-ɧádd issā3a ɧadā3iš, until eleven o’clock.
Before a whole sentence, until is la-3índ ma: la-3índ ma -txarrájit, until I graduated.

data.title: 3úmri: age, and “ever”
points: Age is 3úmr with an ending (chapter 2): 3úmri 3išrīn, I’m 20, word for word my age twenty. To ask: gaddēš 3úmrak?
To turn an age, use ʂār, to become: ɧáyʂīr 3úmru 3išrīn sána, he’s turning twenty.
Before a past verb, 3úmr- means ever: 3úmrak sāfarit gábil hēk?, have you ever been abroad? With ma it means never: 3úmri ma sāfárit…, I’ve never flown…

data.title: lābis, sākin: words for a state
points: Many verbs have a describing word in one shape: lābis, wearing; sākin, living (somewhere); nāyim, asleep; rāyiɧ, going; 3āyiš, living.
It says the state you’re in now, with no b-: lābis naɖɖārāt ilyōm?, are you wearing glasses today? wēn sākin?, where do you live?
It changes like a describing word: rāyiɧ for a man, rāyɧa for a woman or a feminine thing, lābsīn for several.
Hebrew’s present tense is this same kind of word. Arabic lābis has the shape of Hebrew לובש.

data.title: áɧmar, ɧámra: colors and looks
points: Colors and how someone looks share one shape, with a- in front: áɧmar, red; ásmar, dark-skinned; á3ma, blind; áʂla3, bald.
For a woman or a feminine thing, the a- goes and -a comes at the end: ɧámra, sámra, 3ámya. For several: ɧúmur, súmur, 3imyān.
It follows the word it describes: šá3arha ášgar, her hair is blond, since šá3ar, hair, is masculine.
Hebrew gives these a shape of their own too: עִוֵּר, blind; אִלֵּם, mute.

data.title: ja3ān, šab3ān: hungry and full
points: Many words for how your body feels end in -ān: ja3ān, hungry; 3aʈšān, thirsty; šab3ān, full; ta3bān, tired. For a woman they end in -āna.
Each has a verb for getting that way: jā3, to get hungry; 3íʈiš, to get thirsty; šíbi3, to get full.
The past of that verb says how you are now: šbí3it, I’m full, word for word I got full. Hebrew does the same with שבעתי.

data.title: máʈbax, máɣsala: where it’s done
points: ma- in front of a verb’s root names the place where it’s done: máʈbax, kitchen (ʈábax, to cook); mál3ab, playground (lí3ib, to play); máktab, office (kátab, to write); mádrasa, school (dáras, to study).
Some name a thing it’s done in or with: máɣsala, sink (ɣásal, to wash); múknisa, broom.
Their plurals share one shape: maʈābix, malā3ib, makātib, maɣāsil.
Hebrew builds the same way: מִטְבָּח from טבח, and mádrasa is Hebrew’s מדרשה.

data.title: ráfa3, názzal: old verbs, new jobs
points: Screens took their verbs from everyday life. ráfa3 lifts (ráfa3 īdu, he raised his hand) and also uploads; názzal lowers (názzal iššubbāk, he rolled the window down) and also downloads.
fátaɧ opens a door, a file, or the internet: fátaɧ innít, to go online. sákkar closes a program, and sákkar ilxáʈʈ hangs up the phone.
šáɣɣal starts a car, turns on a computer, and plays a song.
Hebrew did the same: להוריד, to bring down, also downloads, and להעלות, to bring up, uploads.

data.title: xallīna: “let’s”
points: xallīna and a verb with no b- means let’s: xallīna núg3ud bárra, let’s sit outside.
The verb after it starts with n-, for we: nrūɧ, níšrab, núg3ud.
It comes from xálla, to let or allow: xallīna is word for word let us. It can stand alone: xallīna júwwa, let’s stay inside.

data.title: ɧáda, íši: “someone”, “something”
points: ɧáda is someone and íši is something: fī ɧáda 3a -lbāb, someone is at the door; bíddi ākul íši ɧílu, I want to eat something sweet.
ayy before them makes any: ayy ɧáda, anyone; ayy íši, anything.
kull íši is everything (chapter 24). With not, íši means anything at all: mā fhímtiš íši, I didn’t understand a thing.

data.title: janūbi: the -i ending
points: Add -i to a word to get a describing word from it: janūb, south; janūbi, southern. šamāli is northern; dáwli is international.
Languages and peoples work the same way: 3árabi, Arabic.
With il-, both words take it (chapter 32): ilqúʈb iššamāli, the North Pole.
Hebrew has the same ending. Hebrew דרומי is southern, from דרום.

data.title: najjār, xabbāz: the job shape
points: Many jobs have one shape, a doubled middle and a long ā: xabbāz, baker; najjār, carpenter; rassām, painter (of art); bayyā3, shop assistant.
It comes from what the person does: rásam, to draw, gives rassām; bā3, to sell, gives bayyā3; sāg, to drive, gives sawwāg tāksi, taxi driver.
Hebrew has this shape too, and najjār is the same word as Hebrew נגר, a carpenter.

data.title: tult, rúbi3: parts, and sums
points: A part is named from its number’s root: talāta, three → tult, a third; árba3a, four → rúbi3, a quarter. A half is nuʂʂ.
Hebrew does the same: שליש, a third, comes from שלוש, three, and רבע, a quarter, from ארבע, four.
Sums: zāʔid, plus; nāgiʂ, minus; ɖarb, times; taqsīm, divided by. Equals is bisāwi or bíʈla3: talāta ɖarb árba3a bisāwi tnā3iš, three times four is twelve.

data.title: batmánna and yā rēt: “I hope”, “I wish”
points: batmánna, I hope, takes a verb with no b-: batmánna ʔašūfak márra tānya, I hope to see you again.
For not, put mā before the verb: batmánna mā yʂīrlu íši, I hope nothing happens to him.
yā rēt, I wish, is for what isn’t so: yā rēt kúnit fi falasʈīn, I wish I were in Palestine. With law (chapter 22): yā rēt law 3índi sayyāra, I wish I had a car.
yā rēt is Hebrew’s הלוואי.

data.title: ta3ālib, ɖafāɖi3: the plural of a four-letter root
points: A word with four root letters makes its plural on one shape, a-ā-i: tá3lab → ta3ālib, foxes; ɖúfɖa3 → ɖafāɖi3, frogs; sulɧufā → salāɧif, turtles.
Longer words fit the shape too, and drop what’s left over: 3ankabūt → 3anākib, spiders.
A long vowel at the end stays long, as ī: dulfīn → dalāfīn, dolphins.
You’ve met the shape already: maʈābix, kitchens (chapter 40).
Some of these are old relatives: tá3lab is Hebrew’s שועל, fox, and ɖúfɖa3 is its צפרדע, frog.

data.title: dáxxan, tadxīn, mudáxxin: one verb, three words
points: A verb with a doubled middle (chapter 20) makes its -ing word with ta- and a long ī: dáxxan, to smoke; tadxīn, smoking. The same way: tawqī3, a signature; ta3līm, education; tadrīb, practice.
The one who does it starts with mu-: mudáxxin, a smoker.
Hebrew’s piʿel does the same. Hebrew מעשן is a smoker.

data.title: mʂálliɧ, muwáʐʐaf: the doer and the done-to
points: The mu- word of a doubled-middle verb (chapter 52) has two faces, one vowel apart. With i, it’s the one who does it: mʂálliɧ, a repairman (ʂállaɧ, to fix); muɧárrir, an editor.
With a, it’s the one it’s done to: muwáʐʐaf, an employee, the one employed (wáʐʐaf, to employ); msákkar, closed (sákkar, to close); mɧámmar, roasted.
In speech mu- often shrinks to m-: mʂálliɧ, msákkar.
Hebrew splits the same way: מנהל is a manager, and מנוהל is managed.

data.title: 3índu, má3u: being ill
points: Many illnesses take 3ind- (chapter 8): 3índu rábu, he has asthma; 3índu ɖáɣiʈ, he has high blood pressure.
Some take ma3-, with: má3u súkkar, he’s diabetic; má3u ʔinfluwánza, he has the flu. Learn each one with its own.
For an ache, the part that hurts does the hurting: rāsu ʔája3u, he has a headache, word for word his head hurts him. Pointing: fī wája3 hān, it hurts here.

data.title: ittáffag ma3, jādal 3ála: a verb and its little word
points: Many verbs come with a little word, learned together: ittáffag ma3, to agree with; jādal 3ála, to argue about; ɧass b-, to feel; xáʈʈaʈ la-, to plan on.
It isn’t always the one English uses: radd 3ála, to answer (word for word, to answer on); fāz 3ála, to beat a team; itfárraj 3ála, to watch.
That’s why a verb’s card shows its little word in both forms: ittáffag ma3, yittíffig ma3.
Hebrew does this too: להסכים עם is to agree with, and להתווכח על is to argue about.

data.title: wāfag, ywāfig: a verb comes in pairs
points: Each verb is given in two forms, he did and he does: wāfag, ywāfig, to approve of. The b- of chapter 7 goes on the second: biwāfig, he approves.
The vowel in the second form can’t be guessed from the first: níjiɧ, yínjaɧ, to succeed; ámar, yúʔmur, to order. Learn the pair together.
A long ā in the middle changes in the second form: rāɧ, yrūɧ, to go; bā3, ybī3, to sell.
Hebrew dictionaries list a verb by he did too.

data.title: tālit, rābi3: first, second, third
points: First is áwwal (ūla for a feminine thing). From second to tenth, the number takes the shape tālit: tāni, tālit, rābi3, xāmis, up to 3āšir.
For a feminine thing they end in -a: tālta, rāb3a. ilqanā -ttālta, channel 3.
After the thing, with il- on both (chapter 32): iʈʈābig irrābi3, the fourth floor. Before it, with no il-: 3āšir sána, the tenth year.

data.title: gaddēš ɧájim: “how big” is “how much size”
points: Where English says how and a describing word, Arabic asks how much of the thing, with gaddēš (chapter 26): gaddēš ɧájim dārku?, how big is your house? Word for word, how much size.
The same for how far: gaddēš ilmasāfa min hān la-lbálad?, how far is it to downtown? (how much is the distance).
How often is every how much: kull gaddēš bitmárran?, how often do you exercise?
Hebrew asks one this way too: כמה זמן, how long, is how much time.

data.title: wála íši: “nothing”, “no one”
points: wála before ɧáda or íši makes no one, nothing: wála ɧáda, no one; wála ʔíši, nothing.
It works as a whole answer: šū -štarēt? – wála ʔíši, what did you buy? – Nothing!
In a sentence, fiš ɧadd says no one: fiš ɧadd bi3īš la-lʔábad, no one lives forever. kull wāɧad is everyone, and ayy ɧáda is anyone (chapter 45).

data.title: álla ywáffgak: wishing someone well
points: Many wishes are álla, God, and a verb with no b-: álla ywáffgak, good luck (word for word, God make you succeed); álla yišfīk, get well soon.
The ending says who it’s for (chapter 14): álla yírɧamu, may he rest in peace; álla yirɧámha, for a woman.
Thanks are often a wish too: álla ybārik fīk, God bless you, which is also how you answer mabrūk, congratulations.
Hebrew’s blessing יְבָרֶכְךָ, may He bless you, wishes with the same y- in front.
